The One Who Lied
Where the Story Broke
I stood on the step and counted it on my fingers, which is where I keep my best work.
I leaned on the wall for a minute. The wall didn’t mind, and I needed the company.
I stopped under a street lamp and went over it, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong.
I went over what I had, which is the part of the job where you find out how little that is.
I took stock. It didn’t take long, which was either a good sign or the other kind.
I went over it from the top, slowly, the way a man reads his own handwriting.
I filed it at a quarter to eight and went home the long way. The city was waking up and didn’t want to hear about it.
The DA’s man read it twice, which is once more than he reads most things, and put it in the basket that matters.
{client} took the news the way people take good news at eight in the morning: suspiciously, and with coffee.
I told {client} who, and where, and {client} went to get it back with a look on {cHis} face I wouldn’t have wanted to be on the other end of.
It was most of the answer. Most of an answer is what this city usually settles for, and it settled.
I had the who and not all the rest. The rest is the part that holds up in daylight.
I filed the wrong name. **The wrong name is a name somebody has to live with.** I went home and didn’t sleep, which seemed fair.
The name I wrote down was the wrong one. **Somebody who did nothing is going to have a very bad morning on my account.**
Eight o’clock came and I had nothing to put on the page. Nothing files itself. It just goes cold.
I left the name blank. A blank is honest, which is the best thing anybody said about it.

The Story Comes Apart
Somebody Wasn’t There
An Hour Gone Missing
Not Where They Said
The First Crack
I went out onto the landing and stood there a minute, putting the night in order like a man sorting his socks.
I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you count change you don’t trust.
I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order.
I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest.
I sat down on the stairs, which were the only thing in the building that didn’t want something from me.
I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to.
I went over what I had. It fitted on one page, with room left for a sandwich.
I took out the notebook and read it from the top, as if somebody else had written it.
I stopped to go over what I had, before there was any more of it.
I went over the night from the beginning, every name and every hour, slowly.
I sat on a step and went through it all again, start to finish.
I took stock, which in my line of work means counting what you know, then counting what you don’t, and coming up short on both.
I put the name in the report and the report on the desk of a man who could do something about it. {client} heard about it on the telephone at breakfast.
It was done by daylight. I took {client} through it over coffee, and {client} listened to all of it without once putting the cup down.
The police took the name, and after an hour of telling me how they’d have got there anyway, they took the rest.
I filed it and went home past the milk wagons. Somewhere behind me, a door was going to get a knock it had been expecting.
By the afternoon everything was back where it belonged, and {client} was telling the neighbours it had never been in doubt.
I told {client} the whole of it. {client} listened, nodded and put the kettle on, which on that street is the highest honour there is.
It was a small thing, as these things go, but it wasn’t small to {client}, and it was put right.
I told {client} who, and where, and why. {client} took it in quietly and went to get {cHis} coat.
I had the who and a fair part of the rest. It would do, the way a coat with one button does.
It was most of the answer, and I filed it as most of an answer. Somebody else would have to find the rest, or nobody would.
{client} read it and said it was more than {client} had had before. That’s a kind thing to say about a report with holes in it.
I had the right name and not everything that went with it. Some of the night would stay where I’d left it.
I put a name in the report, and it was the wrong one. **Somebody who did nothing will spend the next year explaining it to people who won’t believe a word.**
The name I filed was a name, and that was all it was. **An innocent person is going to lose a job, a room and most of their friends over my handwriting.**
I filed it feeling sure, which is the worst way to be wrong. **Somebody innocent will wake up to a knock at the door, and I’m the one who sent it.**
I got the wrong one. **A person who never did a thing will have a policeman at the door and the whole street at the windows, on my word.**
I didn’t put down a name. A guess is worse than nothing, and nothing was what I had.
Morning came and found me with a lot of evenings written down and nobody to put at the end of them.
I left the name blank and told {client} so. {client} took it better than I did.
The report went in with a blank where the name goes. A blank never hurt anybody. That’s the best you can say for it, and the worst.
